questions.q: According to this lesson, what does "dashboard storytelling" actually mean in practice?
options: Controlling the order in which a viewer's eye lands on information, using layout, KPI placement, and actions built earlier in this chapter
Adding more decorative annotations and a dramatic color scheme to every dashboard
Writing a text narrative that replaces all charts on the dashboard
A Tableau-specific feature you enable from a menu
questions.explain: Storytelling is treated as a concrete, learnable structural skill — using KPI headers, layout, actions, and dynamic titles to guide attention in a deliberate order, not adding more decoration.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the concrete decluttering rules given in this lesson?
options: Every color needs a reason — if a color legend doesn't map to something the viewer needs to distinguish, it's noise
Every dashboard should use as many colors as possible to look more professional
White space should always be eliminated to fit more charts on screen
Filters should be placed as far as possible from what they affect
questions.explain: The lesson's decluttering rules include: every color needs a reason, filters should be visible near what they affect, white space isn't wasted space, and unexplainable elements should be removed.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a common real cause of a slow-feeling dashboard?
options: A live connection to a slow source query that re-runs on every filter change
Using an extract instead of a live connection
Setting a Range size instead of Automatic
Using context filters instead of regular quick filters
questions.explain: A live connection re-querying a slow source on every interaction is a common performance culprit — the fix suggested is switching to an extract where live data isn't strictly required.

questions.q: Why does switching non-essential actions from Hover to Select help dashboard performance?
options: Select fires far less often than Hover, which triggers on every pointer movement across a mark
Select and Hover have identical performance characteristics, so it makes no difference
Hover-triggered actions are not supported in Tableau at all
Select disables all data queries entirely
questions.explain: Hover fires continuously as the pointer passes over marks, which can mean many simultaneous action evaluations; Select only fires on a deliberate click, reducing how often the dashboard has to recompute.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about the relationship between dashboard performance and earlier chapters (like extracts, context filters, and sizing)?
options: A slow dashboard is very often a symptom of a decision made several chapters earlier, not a Tableau limitation — performance ties directly back to those earlier concepts
Performance has nothing to do with any decision made before Chapter 14
Context filters and extracts were deprecated once dashboards were introduced
Only dashboard sizing affects performance; connection type and filters do not
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties performance back to extracts vs. live connections (Chapter 2), context filters (Chapter 5), and dashboard sizing (Lesson 79) — performance is often a downstream consequence of earlier design choices, which Chapter 16 goes deeper on.
